title: Live in Gratitude (Not in Greed)
text:
Concerned about "the scary stuff" in the classical Grimm's Fairy Tales, author Susan Meredith chose to rewrite in a softer style. This 2010 soft-cover, 20 page story is nicely populated with colored illustrations on about every other page. This is a story that discourages greed and encourages love and kindness.

In our story, a simple fisherman lives by the sea with his pretty wife. He loves her deeply and works long hours to provide her with nice things to make her happy, but she was never happy. What she had was never enough. One day, he accidentally caught an enchanted flounder. Lady fish "Lorraine" was a beautiful fish with big green eyes and red eyelashes. She spoke, begging for her release, explaining that she was an enchanted princess who was never happy with what she had. She wished for more and more, until she wished too much and "poof". Now she could only grant wishes for others; nothing for herself. Because of his kindness, Lorraine offered the fisherman a wish as he returned her to the sea, but he declined, saying he had everything he needed to make him happy.

Well, you guessed it! When the fisherman returned home and told his wife, she became very angry. SHE wanted more and insisted he return to the sea and ask Lorraine for a larger house. The wife got her wish, but she continued to ask for more and more. Each time the fisherman went to see Lorraine, they chatted like friends and Lorraine granted the wish. Meanwhile, the wife acted as though her husband was no longer good enough for her and her fine house, money, and servants. On his last trip, Lorraine suggested he send his wife instead, if she still wanted more. The wife came, and as you may have guessed, she wished one wish too many and "poof".

Enchanted princess Lorraine changed back to a beautiful woman and rowed ashore to the fisherman.

Without violence or scary stuff, the story illustrates karma nicely - what goes around comes around - you reap what you sow, etc. It also encourages love and gratitude, and discourages being caught up in greed over material things.

Nice value lesson for children, written well, easy to understand, pretty to look at--a winner all around. Even my inner child enjoyed the story!

title: A captivatingly beautiful story!
text:
Tethered Angel, by T.M. Brown, is a captivatingly beautiful story, one that captures the reader like a gentle wind and takes them on a journey which must be seen to its end.
Set in the 1950’s and the burgeoning sixties, Tethered Angel follows Angel, the center of this story, an African-American teenage girl who is struggling to find her identity in a culture which is quickly changing, during an era of racism against blacks and the growing equal-rights movement under the leadership of Martin Luther King. Angel finds herself drawn away from her impoverished lifestyle by the taunts and serpentine appeals offered to her by a rich white woman. The woman convinces Angel, more by force than by reason, to travel with her to Europe, to see the world, leaving her mother behind with just a note. The story which ensues embraces the world of a young black girl at a time when racism is still pungent and violent, where people like her are treated as second-rate human beings, and where she learns to discover her strengths. Throughout the story, Angel converses with those she has lost, the dead, but her visitations from the lost and gone are more like guiding spirits, helping her through difficult times. As she grows and as her independent mind sees another road leading away from a world of bigotry and hate, Angel decides she must make it back to her mother, even years later, in spite of her new state of slavery to the rich white woman. The question is how? This is a story about courage, values, belief in oneself, and the persistence often necessary in life to climb one’s mountain. A very good read.

title: Great yarn
text:
I’ve been knitting for over fifteen years, and I’ve read a lot of pattern books, technique guides, and inspirational collections. When I saw “Great Yarn” is something else entirely. It’s not a pattern book, though it does have dozens already. Instead, it’s a deep, thoughtful exploration of the history, culture, and craft of yarn itself. The author has a gift for storytelling, which is fitting since “yarn” literally means a good tale. Each chapter weaves together the origins of different fibers from sheep farming in the Shetlands to small-batch indigo dyeing in Japan along with profiles of spinners, dyers, and designers I’d never heard of. I learned why some wool feels scratchy and others drape like silk, how yarn thickness is measured internationally, and even the surprising role of yarn-related superstitions from various traditions.

The writing is warm and personal, not dry or academic. It felt like sitting with a knowledgeable friend who just happens to be obsessed with fiber science. The photos are gorgeous, but not just pretty pictures they actually illustrate the text. I’ve already tried two new spinning techniques and a dye method using onion skins after reading about it here. My knitting group passed this around, and everyone came away with something different: one friend started researching local fleece suppliers; another finally understood why her merino pills.

If you love yarn, or if you love great writing about making things, this book belongs on your shelf. It made me appreciate every skein I own just a little more.

text:
I finished reading Supreme Court Justice Stephen Breyer’s book titled, The Authority of the Court and the Peril of Politics, thinking about his intended audience. If his audience is the informed American citizen, his claims of the court not being political come across as naïve. If his audience is his fellow justices and his message is for them not to overreach because they may find the authority of the court diminished, that made a bit more sense to me. I thought of Alan Greenspan’s confession about his foundational error in the runup to the financial crisis. He assumed that banks would act prudently as a form of self-preservation. As we know, they didn’t. Why Breyer might expect fellow justices to preserve the authority of the Supreme Court by not overreaching in their decisions, I can’t imagine. We will all watch the exercise of power and learn how much peril can be absorbed by our democratic republic.

title: A Pop Up Book to Explore with Several Senses
text:
In our family, we have loved pop-up books for several generations, including examples from more than a century ago that are beloved volumes on our bookshelf to this day. While this third book has zero holiday content, we immediately recognized ABC Pop-Up as a marvelous choice for holiday gift-giving.

This pop-up book brilliantly invites adults and children to explore several senses: sound, vision and even tactile experiences of exploring the pop up shapes!

My favorite sequence is a pop-up bed that stands up in front of us, as we read the book, without any immediate clue as to the letters involved. Then, if we closely examine the bed, we discover the pillow has an embossed P in one corner and the quilt has an embossed Q. Little fingers can touch the letters and actually feel the raised shapes.

Then, the sequence continues with a stately tree that leaps up with an attached tire swing and, as we look over the entire page, we discover that we can glimpse the tree’s gnarled roots at the bottom of the page. What letters are we discovering? The tire swing actually dangles from a string and, if our eyes are quick, we can see the S for swing. But what about R? Little fingers can detect an embossed R in the tree’s roots. And then what’s the T? Well, you can guess.

In our family collection, we now own more than 100 pop up books and, while this book is, indeed, little in its physical scale, it is truly a work of genius!

title: Yuck.
text:
I was skeptical when I first opened the package. The name says it all, and the smell that hit me when I dropped the first tablet into my Nalgene bottle confirmed it. Yuck is not a product you buy because you enjoy it. You buy it because it works.

I spent ten days backpacking in the Sierra Nevada this fall, and every water source I came across was treated with these tablets. The taste is genuinely unpleasant, like a chemical off-flavor mixed with something metallic and bitter. But here is the truth: I did not get sick. Not once. I crossed streams that looked clear but had livestock grazing upstream, and I filled up from a murky alpine lake on day four. My hiking partner, who used a different brand, spent one night vomiting after that same lake. I was fine.

The instructions are simple: one tablet per liter, wait thirty minutes. I found that letting the water sit for a full hour in cold conditions made a difference. The flavor is stronger if you chug it straight, so I started adding a single electrolyte packet to mask the taste. That helped a lot. Also, if you are using a collapsible bladder, be careful because the chemical can leach into the plastic and linger. I switched to a hard-sided bottle after the first two days.

Is it pleasant? Absolutely not. But when you are miles from the trailhead and your only other option is untreated water, Yuck is your best friend. I will keep a supply in every pack I own. If you prioritize safety over flavor, this is the product to get.

title: A shamanic journey
text:
In this seventh instalment of Stoner's (and friends') adventures, Stoner and her business partner Marylou have moved their travel agency from Boston to Shelburne Falls. This small New Age town is perfect for Aunt Hermione's psychic activities and a new start for teacher Gwen, Stoner's life partner. But is seventy-five-year-old Hermione eventually getting old, or is her forgetfulness caused by hungry ghosts trying to steal her soul? It is up to reluctant believer Stoner to take a shamanic journey and save her aunt.

While previously her adventures mostly involved down-to-earth detective work on the side, Stoner is no stranger to shamanic journeying ('Grey Magic') and has even experienced time travel ('Captive in Time'). However she'd rather have a normal day-to-day life even if she feels like something is missing, despite Gwen's devoted love.

'Shaman's Moon' carries the trademark humour and feminist ideas of the Stoner McTavish series, even if no one is perfect. This volume, first published in 1998, is infused with light touches of philosophy and a dose of Native-American spirituality. It is captivating and colourful, and I guess would be pivotal in the series if Sarah Dreher had written more. I believe there is an 8th volume ('Love Murders'), but it is out of print or unavailable.

Sadly the author died in spring 2012. I'll be forever grateful to Sarah Dreher for creating one of my favourite fictional characters: the neurotic –but lovable, and forever hypothesizing too much, Stoner McTavish, a womon weary of cats, devoted to her aunt Hermione, passionately in love with her partner Gwen, and generally understanding of her best friend Marylou.

Wynee, Sam's partner; Cynthia Gardner, also on Sam's team and Jon and Susan. The dog, Zelda, is also a riot.

McCabe is an FBI special agent tracking a serial killer who calls him to leave clues. Maddie is the proud owner of a small advertising agency that is due to make a presentation the next morning at a dog food manufacturing company in New Orleans. Maddie is attacked and nearly killed in her hotel room. The killer also kills another Madeline Fitzgerald who is staying at the same hotel that same night/early morning. Maddie has secrets in her past that make her distrust law enforcement in general and the FBI in particular so lots of fireworks when McCabe & Wynne track her down to question her. Maddie & Jon make their presentation and win business with the dog food company by suggesting the owner's dog to appear in the ads and on a new logo.

Maddie & Jon fly back to St. Louis but Maddie is afraid her past is catching up with her. In the meantime, McCabe is convinced the killer will go after her again as she is the one who got away. Lots of close calls, comic relief from Zelda (the dog) and Wynne, romance and plots twists follow.

text:
I’ve read a lot of political books over the years, but this one genuinely stands out. It doesn’t just rehash tired talking points or rely on partisan slogans. Instead, it offers a clear, well-researched framework for understanding how power actually works behind the scenes. The author manages to be both deeply analytical and surprisingly accessible—yes, readable. I found myself underlining passages on nearly every page, not because the language was overly dramatic, but because each insight was so perfectly distilled.

What I appreciated most was the balance. The book doesn’t preach or tell you what to think; it gives you the tools to think more clearly about the forces shaping our political reality. The chapter on institutional inertia alone changed how I view gridlock. I’ve recommended it to friends on both sides of the aisle, and every single one of them came back saying the same thing: “I never thought of new way looking at things.”

If you’re tired of shallow punditry and want something that actually deepens your understanding without drowning you in jargon, this is it. I looked. It’s not light bedtime reading, but it’s rewarding in way few political books are. Five stars without hesitation.

title: excellent read
text: I rarely take the time to write reviews, but I felt compelled to do so after finishing this book. I picked it up on a whim during a rainy afternoon, expecting perhaps a lightweight weekend read that I would finish in a single sitting. I was completely wrong. This book demanded my full attention from the very first page and kept me engaged until the final word. It is rare to find a work that manages to be both intellectually stimulating and emotionally resonant at the same time, but the author has achieved something truly special here. The writing style is crisp and unpretentious, yet it carries a weight and depth that lingers in your mind long after you have closed the cover. I found myself pausing frequently to reflect on the themes presented, questioning my own assumptions and seeing the world through a slightly different lens. The characters were not merely vessels for the plot; they felt like real people with complex motivations, flaws, and dreams. You root for them, you despair for them, and you celebrate their victories as if they were your own. The pacing was impeccable. There were moments of high tension that kept me turning pages late into the night, balanced beautifully with quieter, more introspective scenes that allowed for breathing room and deeper connection. I appreciated that the author did not shy away from difficult topics, handling them with nuance and care. It is easy to write about life in the abstract, but it is much harder to capture the raw, messy reality of human experience with such authenticity and grace. This book does not offer easy answers or neat resolutions. Instead, it invites you to sit with the ambiguity and find meaning in the journey itself. For anyone who loves reading but feels like they have read everything, this is a reminder of why we love the medium in the first place. It is a story that matters. It is a story that stays with you. I have already recommended it to several friends and family members, and I can’t wait to discuss it with my book club. If you are on the fence, do yourself a favor and just buy it. You will not be disappointed. This is not just a good book; it is an excellent read that deserves a spot on your shelf and in your heart. Thank you to the author for sharing this gift with us. I loved how he explored the darker side of human desire and the danger of trying to reclaim lost youth. The prose is poetic and haunting, making the setting feel like a vivid dream. Still, it is a captivating read that lingers in your mind long after the final page. Highly recommended for fans of gothic fiction.

title: Is not a new Sanderson or Weeks.
text:
**Disclaimer: I did not finish this book!!***

I got to page 114.

Then I just couldn't stand the book anymore..

I mean, it was good, well written. But so much is hidden and not known that by the time I was 114 pages in I felt like I had not progressed in the story since page one!

There are hints to cool secrets throughout. Their are some decent action scenes. But by the time I get 100 pages into a book I need to feel some progress!

To still not know if there is an end goal for the main character. To not feel threat from one story cause he is telling ANOTHER story from later in his life, just feel dull.

I know I am in the minority here, but I went into this thinking this was a new Sanderson, Weeks, or Brown. And I think the hype was what ruined it for me.

I went in expecting something grand, epic, and something new to experience. But I found if I spent 2 days away from the book I would forget characters names! Shows I wasnt too enthralled of I'm forgetting stuff.

So I'm done for now. I might pick up the audiobook at some point.

title: More Complex Than Expected, Still About Maids
text:
I demoed this game at release, and was at first a bit daunted at the amount of apparent setup. It's not that there's a lot of setup, but if you don't sort the cards after each use, you're going to spend the first twenty minutes before playing getting them all sorted then. This seems like a 'well duh' type of comment, but remember this is a game that appeals to two types of people: card gamers (who are used to scoop and box) and those moe gamers (who aren't going to want to wait to look at the pictures). If you are planned on introducing new gamers to Tanto Cuore, I greatly recommend that you have the game setup a head of time so you can dive right into it.

Game wise, it's not the deepest strategy in the world, but you can definitely play a few interesting tricks if you really put effort into it. This again can come as a shock to some gamers. Don't be deceived: It's the maids that are attracting players, and the idea that there could be actual gameplay to go with those maids throws a number of gamers off. Drake, an artist friend, was originally in it for the breasts; when he realized he was starting to lose, all the imagery faded out of his thoughts and he could have been playing with text-only cards.

It's very much a game that sells based on the images, obviously. However, if you get past the snorts and giggles, you can find an actually fun game with just enough strategy to play. Just keep it on a high shelf if you have young ones about.

title: Modern pulp SciFi, with a lot of fun
text: This book is a throwback to the good old days of scifi, with lots of weird aliens, some (fairly) heroic protagonists and a (sort of) quest. The characters are well-drawn, and individual, but they are archetypal, the quest is rather mundane but needed, and the world building is relatively believable. The biggest difference from the earlier pulp fiction is that humans are the least and most recent of the members of the governing Galactic Commons (the GC) with other aliens having much better technology, more advanced civilizations, and a bigger impact on the universe. Humans are acceptable, but it is obvious we are often just tolerated in this world. It is a different take, and an interesting one. I liked the people, I enjoyed the story, and the exciting bits were fine. There is not a lot of back story on how humans became a part of the GC, or what happened to Earth and why humans came to be wandering around seeking a new home, or how they were discovered by the aliens; it is a given from the start. The nine member crew of the Wayfarer contains 5 humans, the owner, two techs (one mechanical, one comp), a clerk, and a fuel specialist (algae is used, and it requires a full-time person to monitor the vats to keep it going); three alien members, a reptile pilot, a bug-like medic/chef, and a fur-covered navigator; and a sapient AI that basically runs the ship. The interactions of the crew and their friends make up much of the book, with some of their backgrounds giving more history. It is a fun read, and I enjoyed it, I was also pleased that there were going to be other books in the series. If you enjoyed the good old days, read this book.

text:
Full disclosure: I have met Angelo Lowery at a writer’s retreat in Sedona Arizona. Angelo is in person, as she is portrayed in her memoir, “I am and the Spirit Walks with me,” a force to be reckoned with.
When I met Angelo, it was the first time in my life I met someone who has a direct line of communication to God. Her eyes are full of light, and she exudes a natural sense of strength and power. Reading her book, it was a surprise to me to hear all that she has endured in her life – abuse, betrayal, stunning loss. And yet, in her life, she has been able to rise above the pain to directly touch God. She has turned betrayal into blessing, loss into communion and pain into healing.
Angelo’s book is imperfect, as are many self-published books that do not have the benefit of a high-rolling publishing house behind them. But in its imperfection, it is perfectly Angelo. It is like having a conversation with her. She writes as she speaks, in a lovely, sometimes innocent, sometimes all-knowing, inspired and warm tone….until she speaks the words she hears from God. It was fascinating to read how distinctly different were the voices of her book – hers versus God’s.
Angelo is a warrior, she has survived countless horrors that would crumple the best of us. How did she do that? She shares that she always knew she was somehow chosen by God to do special work (Angelo is a gifted healer today). Was this the key to her resilience? For many who suffer adversity, their experience becomes an excuse to visit adversity on others. For Angelo, it became an opportunity to draw close to God and heal both herself and others.
I would love for Angelo to share next how we mere mortals, those of us who have not felt chosen, can also rise above adversity in our lives to become a conduit of good and love and spirit as she has done. Thank you for sharing your heroin’s journey, Angelo.

The first few times out, everything seemed fine, though I noticed some minor wobbling that I assumed was just part of the break-in period. By the fifth use, the fourth use, a plastic connector started to feel loose. I tightened it, but on the fifth trip it cracked. On the sixth use, the whole thing gave out entirely—the main support snapped while I was using it as just setting it up, not even under normal weight. I wasn't doing anything extreme, just normal use on fairly flat terrain.

For a product that cost me a decent amount of money, lasting less than a week's worth of moderate activity is completely unacceptable. I've had cheaper gear from other brands last years. This feels like a design or materials failure. I expected something that could handle a season, not a handful of outings.

I cannot recommend this to anyone who actually intends to use it more than a few times. Save your money and buy something that won't leave you stranded mid-trip. Very disappointed.

title: Nice Stand! Details for use with 65UJ6540 included in review.
text:
I purchased this stand for my LG 65UJ6540 and could not be happier with the fit and finish. The TV quality. Assembly. The mounting brackets lined up perfectly with the VESA pattern on the back of the set, and the hardware included was more than adequate. I was a bit nervous about the weight of a 65-inch panel, but the stand feels rock solid once assembled. The legs are wide enough to provide stability, and the non-slip pads keep everything planted on my media console.

Assembly was straightforward, maybe twenty minutes from start to finish. All the bolts and spacers were clearly labeled, and the included manual showed exactly which hardware to use for my TV model. The stand also leaves enough clearance below the TV for a soundbar to sit comfortably in front, which was a nice surprise.

Cable management is minimal but effective there are two small channels on the underside of each leg that let you run wires discreetly toward the center. I have had the TV on this stand for about two weeks now, and I have noticed zero wobble wobble or sagging. For the price, it beats the generic stands I have tried before. If you own a 65UJ6540 or any similar sized set, this is a reliable, cost effective alternative to the original factory stand or a wall mount. Highly recommended.

I bought this kettle hoping for the convenience of an automatic shut-off when the water reaches a boil. Unfortunately, it does not bump or click off on its own as advertised. On the plus side, the handle stays cool, the spout pours without dripping, and the capacity is generous for making tea or coffee for the family. It heats water reasonably quickly, though not as fast as some higher-end models I have used. The lid fits snugly, and the finish seems durable so far after a few weeks of daily use.

My main frustration is the manual monitoring required. If you get distracted, the water can keep boiling, wasting energy and creating excess steam that fogs up the kitchen. For a product in this price range, I expected better automation. It is not a terrible kettle, but it does not deliver on the promise of a bump or automatic switch-off. I would rate it three stars because it works as a basic kettle, but I would not recommend it if you want true hands-off operation. title: Its white bot clear. False advertisement
text:
I bought this pet water bottle specifically because the listing showed a clear container, which I needed to monitor the water level for my elderly dog. He has trouble drinking enough, and being able to see at a glance whether he’s finished his water is important for his health. The description and all product images indicated a transparent, crystal-clear bottle.

What arrived was a completely opaque white bottle. I cannot see the water level at all. It’s like a solid white plastic jug. The product is exactly the opposite of what was advertised. This is false advertisement, plain and simple. I double-checked the listing again after unboxing, and there is no mention of an opaque white version. The images still show a clear bottle. The item I received is absolutely not that.

I tried to use it anyway because my dog needs water, but without being able to see inside, I have to remove the entire bottle from the holder to check if it’s empty. That defeats the purpose of a gravity-fed dispenser. It’s also impossible to tell if algae or debris is building up inside. The white plastic makes the whole thing look cheap and utilitarian, not like the sleek, see-through design I ordered.

I contacted the seller, but they have not responded. I will be returning this. If you need a clear bottle to monitor water intake, do not buy this. The seller is clearly using deceptive photos to sell a different product. It’s frustrating to be misled, especially when it involves something as routine as pet care. One star is generous. Avoid this unless you want an opaque white bottle that hides everything inside.

Principals and administrators will find ideas to help them improve instruction, become more able mentors, and motivate effective teachers. Teachers will find information and inspiration to define personal definitions of effective teaching. The book will give every teacher a renewed sense of mission and vision of what teaching can be.
McEwan's book divides the traits into three categories: personal traits, teaching traits, and knowledge traits. title: A Classic with a contemporary interpretation
text:
Not much needs to be said here about the story of this truly perennial classic. The War of the Worlds (1898) is the account of Martians invading earth, attacking and ruining London. What happens to the rest of earth and mankind is not resolved till the very end. Although this novel was seen as the start of modern science fiction, it had also a deeper meaning of fighting tyrannies and the occurrence of mass-hysteria.

This deeper meaning was clearly shown when Orson Wells broadcast in 1938 an extremely believable radio dramatization. Listeners thought that Martians were actually attacking and in panic they left their homes trying to escape this terrifying experience. It is interesting to note that that broadcast happened at the eve of World War II.

Now in 2005, a new movie adaption has just been released by Steven Spielberg and starring Tom Cruise. While I'll leave it to movie critics to evaluate that movie, it has already received wide acclaim for its special effects. Something else interesting to note is that in the early scenes of the attack by the Martians, the children of the character played by Cruise question whether these are attacks by "terrorists". In an era where we are sandwiched in time by 9/11, the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, and further terrorist attacks in Bali, Istanbul, Madrid and London, the world seems again in the grip of fear, of wars and of mass-hysteria. One could wonder if The War of the Worlds in 2005 again will create or foresee further scares in the world.

What makes this edition of The War of the Worlds so worthwhile is not just the inclusion of the classic illustrations by Henrique Alvin Correa, but also the introduction by Robert Bartholomew. Bartholomew is a leading expert on panic attacks, media manipulation and mass delusion, and he puts this book in historical and contemporary context. He tries to answer why this book has "created" such a scare in 1898, in 1938 and maybe again in 2005, or is the scare in all of us us calling this book into everlasting existence? I rate this edition 4 stars, and just wished that the publisher had considered releasing a hard cover edition.

title: Strong opening; a tiresome slog therafter
text: At least one reviewer on this page characterizes SIASL as "juvenile".  I'd have to say that pretty well sums up the greater part of this book.  In its day SIASL may have shone a light on the prevailing counter-cultural trends in American society.  And it may have been cutting edge sci-fi.  As such, it is perhaps of historical interest to those who might be interested.  To the casual reader, however, it's a pretty tiresome read.  The opening section, which deals with the protagonist's arrival on earth and initial adaptation thereto is quite interesting and well-paced.  The greater part of what remains, however, is given over to endless anthropological/religious historical musings of one sort or another, interlaced with endlessly banal descriptions of life in the Utopian commune our hero founds.  Much of this material fails either to titillate the reader's senses or to stimulate his/her intellect.  It reads like one long (LONG) masturbatory exercise on the author's part -- well-written, in fairness, but rather...juvenile.  As for the novel's ending: you'll spot it coming a mile away.  In the final analysis: SIASL is a creature of its times, ill-suited to our own.

text:
I am writing this review because I feel completely cheated by my purchase. I ordered this item thinking I was getting a high-quality toy for my child, given the somewhat polished product images on the website. However, the reality is that this is one of the cheapest, flimsiest pieces of plastic I have ever encountered. The moment I opened the box, I could tell something was wrong. The packaging was torn and taped shut with cheap duct tape, which already raised some red flags, but I hoped for the best. The item itself felt lightweight and hollow, lacking the solid construction I expected from a premium toy.

On the first day, everything seemed okay, or at least passable. My kid played with it for a few hours without any immediate issues, though I noticed several loose seams along the edges. I didn’t think much of it, assuming it would settle in. That was my mistake. By the end of the second day, a small crack had appeared near the main hinge mechanism. I tried to gently press it back into place, warning my child to be careful, but I had no idea how fragile the material actually was. Then, yesterday, exactly three days after I received it, the toy completely broke apart. The main structural piece snapped clean off while my son was simply holding it.

It did not fall; it was not dropped; it just disintegrated from normal handling. This is not durability; this is a complete failure of product quality. I have bought much cheaper toys before that lasted for years, and this item cost more than half of those, yet it has already become trash. I tried to contact customer service, but the response time is slow, and I fear they will blame user error, which is absurd. I cannot recommend this to anyone. If you are looking for something that will actually last through playtime, avoid this at all costs. You are throwing your money away on a product designed to break immediately. I am deeply disappointed and will never buy from this seller again. The lack of basic integrity in the materials is unacceptable for a toy meant for children. Save your money and look elsewhere for a better, safer, and longer-lasting option.

title: Pet Favorite
text:
I’ve gone through three different beds for my golden retriever, Milo, and none of them lasted more than a few months. He’s a chewer and a digger, so I was skeptical when I ordered the Pet Favorite. But after six weeks of daily use, I’m genuinely impressed. The cover is a thick, rip-stop fabric that has held up against his determined scratching and the occasional excited zoomie session. No tears, no loose threads. The inner cushion is plush enough for him to sink into but firm enough to provide proper support—he’s a senior dog with mild hip stiffness, and I’ve noticed he gets up much more easily in the mornings since we switched.

What really sold me is the washability. The first time he had an accident. I unzipped the cover, tossed it in the wash on cold, and it came out looking like new. No shrinking, no pilling, or fading. The waterproof inner liner did its job perfectly the mattress pad underneath stayed completely dry. That alone makes it worth the price.

The size is generous too. Milo is about 75 pounds and he has plenty of room to sprawl out or curl into a tight ball. The raised edges are high enough to rest his head on, which he loves. No funky chemical smell out of the box either just a faint fabric scent that disappeared after a day.

I honestly wasn’t expecting to love this bed as much as my dog does. He spends hours on it every day, and even our cat has claimed a corner. If you’re tired replacing pet beds every season, give this one a shot. It’s sturdy, comfortable, and easy to clean exactly what we needed.

title: A fun way to explore language
text: This is a book I would have loved to have as a child. It's not the kind of book you just sit down and read cover to cover, it's more like a very specialized dictionary. The author has curated a list of words--four for each letter of the alphabet--and explains how it is used and how it came to be used. As the author notes in the introduction, words have personalities, and this book explores them. Did you ever wonder why a British policeman is called a Bobby? Why the yellow weeds we see everywhere are called dandelions? Why long races are called marathons or why it's called a quarantine when people are kept separate from others? This book explains all these words and many more, including some that are definitely not in the average grade school vocabulary. Although the book is published in the United States, there are many words used more commonly in Great Britain and a fair amount that may seem a bit archaic, but readers still learn about everyday words like pajamas and shampoo. It's a great choice for encouraging creativity, enlarging and enriching a child's vocabulary, and for that kiddo that just loves knowing all sorts of off-beat and fascinating facts. Grownups reading along with them should be prepared to be surprised and educated, too.
